content: Tobacco is an agricultural product derived from the fresh leaves of plants belonging to the genus Nicotiana. It has been cultivated on the American continent since approximately 6000 BC and was first utilized by native cultures around 3000 BC. Evidence suggests that tobacco has been smoked in various forms since about 2000 BC, with pictorial depictions of ancient Mayans smoking primitive cigars dating back to 1400 BC. Tobacco has a long-standing history of use in Native American cultures and played a significant role in the early economic foundation of the United States, particularly during colonial times and the establishment of the Jamestown settlement. Commercially available tobacco is typically dried, cured, and processed into natural forms. It is most commonly consumed by smoking in the form of cigars, cigarettes, or through devices such as stem pipes, water pipes, or hookahs. Tobacco can also be consumed by chewing, dipping (placing it between the cheek and gum), or sniffing finely powdered snuff into the nose. Many countries enforce a minimum legal smoking age to regulate the purchase and use of tobacco products. Regardless of the method of consumption, tobacco use results in the absorption of varying amounts of nicotine into the bloodstream, leading to the development of tolerance and dependence over time. The degree of dependence and tolerance is influenced by the quantity, frequency, and speed of nicotine absorption. All forms of tobacco consumption introduce nicotine into the bloodstream, albeit in varying amounts. A lethal dose of nicotine can be found in as little as half a cigar or three cigarettes. However, only a small fraction of the nicotine in these products is released into the smoke. Most clinically significant cases of nicotine poisoning arise from concentrated forms of nicotine, such as those used in insecticides. Some reports suggest that even a discarded cigarette butt may contain enough nicotine to be fatal to a small child. In addition to nicotine, tobacco contains other active alkaloids, such as harmala alkaloids. Long-term tobacco use is associated with a significantly increased risk of developing various cancers, strokes, and severe cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. Tobacco smoking has been linked to substantially shorter life expectancies. Research has shown that tobacco use can induce lasting changes in the brain, similar to those caused by substances like morphine or cocaine. To mitigate the public health risks associated with tobacco smoking, many jurisdictions have implemented smoking bans. The heightened risk of cancer associated with tobacco use is largely attributed to the presence of nitrosamines and other carcinogenic compounds formed during anaerobic heating processes, such as smoking, flue-curing, or fire-curing. While the use of flue-cured or fire-cured smokeless tobacco reduces the risk of respiratory cancers compared to smoked tobacco, it still carries a significant risk of oral cancer. In contrast, steam-cured chewing tobacco (snus) avoids the generation of nitrosamines and their associated carcinogenicity, though the adverse effects of nicotine on the cardiovascular system and pancreas remain unmitigated. Tobacco smoking is responsible for the deaths of over 400,000 Americans annually, including 276,000 men and 142,000 women. A study conducted by Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece measured the levels of naturally occurring radium and polonium in Greek tobacco leaves. The radiation dose from these elements was found to be nearly 1,000 times higher than the levels of cesium-137 detected in plant life near the Chernobyl disaster site. Although the radiation dose received by tobacco smokers is only 10% of the average environmental radiation exposure, some scientists believe that this radioactive content is a major contributor to cancer-related deaths in smokers, rather than nicotine or tar. The 12-month prevalence of tobacco use disorder, as defined by DSM-IV criteria, is approximately 13% among individuals aged 18 years and older. Risk factors for developing tobacco use disorder include anxiety disorders, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), bipolar disorder, conduct disorder, depressive disorders, externalizing personality traits, genetic predisposition, low income, low educational attainment, other substance use disorders, personality disorders, and psychotic disorders. Tobacco withdrawal is a recognized condition with a prevalence of approximately 50% in the general population. Differential diagnoses for tobacco withdrawal include anxiety disorders, alcohol withdrawal, bipolar disorder, caffeine withdrawal, caffeine intoxication, depressive disorders, medication-induced akathisia, opioid withdrawal, sedative/hypnotic/anxiolytic withdrawal, stimulant withdrawal, sleep disorders, and voluntary smoking cessation.
